articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter {beacon} Business & Economy Business & Economy The Big Story Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May An international oil benchmark hit $110 per barrel on Friday, as the industry faces persistent shocks from the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars. © Kamran Jebreili, Associated…
articles.body:
Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May

An international oil benchmark hit $110 per barrel on Friday, as the industry faces persistent shocks from the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars.

© Kamran Jebreili, Associated Press file

The price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, hit $110 on the nose during Friday trading. That marked the first time it has reached that level since May 20 , less than three months after the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran conflict.

The commodity is trading at roughly $109.75 as of late Friday afternoon.

Brent crude prices peaked in late April, when the benchmark topped $120 per barrel .

Oil prices shot up during the early months of the conflict with Iran and sunk down below $80 per barrel throughout much of June and July — as the U.S. and Iran were operating under a ceasefire both sides accused the other of violating.

But as the war, now approaching the eight-month mark, has persisted, oil prices have surpassed $100 yet again.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the North American benchmark, also topped $100 per barrel on Friday for the first time since Sep. 21.

The increase in oil prices has translated to higher prices at the pump for Americans. Regular gas in the U.S. costs about $4.33 per gallon on average, AAA reported Friday.

Diesel also costs more than $6.30 on average , nearly $2.70 higher than a year ago, according to AAA.

articles.title: A $2 trillion deficit looms over the midterms
articles.summary: The federal budget deficit rose to nearly $2 trillion for the past fiscal year, which ended September 30, the Treasury Department reported Friday.
articles.body: The federal budget deficit rose to nearly $2 trillion for the past fiscal year, which ended September 30, the Treasury Department reported Friday. It was the largest annual deficit since 2021, during the height of the pandemic, when the federal government doled out support to keep the economy and Americans afloat. This past fiscal year’s deficit was 12% higher than the prior year’s $1.78 trillion gap. Net interest payments on the public debt topped $1 trillion for the first time, driven up in part by the nation’s skyrocketing debt levels and higher interest rates. The United States spent more on interest than on any category other than Social Security and Medicare. The deficit also grew because the Trump administration had to issue refunds after the Supreme Court found that certain global tariffs it imposed violated federal law. The Treasury Department estimates that about $145 billion in tariff refunds was issued in the last fiscal year. Although the economy is in relatively good shape, the nation’s fiscal health has worsened in recent years with neither Republicans nor Democrats on Capitol Hill willing to fully address the issue. “Today’s deficit figures cap off a remarkably dismal year for our fiscal health,” Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement. “Fiscal discipline requires finding something both achievable and aggressive … Tough choices will be needed to get there, and we’re running out of time to make them.” The US debt hit a record $40 trillion in August, a grim milestone that will have consequences for Americans, businesses and the government for years to come. Yet the “big, beautiful bill” that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans enacted last year is expected to add trillions more to the national debt over a decade as its generous tax breaks outweigh the package’s spending cuts. The nation’s growing financial woes, along with rising corporate debt supply and expectations for higher Federal Reserve interest rates, have sparked turmoil in bond markets in recent months. Investors are increasingly jittery, which has sent rates on US debt soaring: The yield on the 10-year Treasury note recently hit its highest level since 2002. That has also led to higher mortgage rates, making it even more difficult to buy and sell homes. With rising deficits, the government has to issue more bonds to fund its spending. Yields on bonds have soared this year as investors demand more compensation to hold US debt. That raises the government’s cost of borrowing, exacerbating concerns about the mounting debt burden. The average weighted interest rate of the debt outstanding was 3.53% at the end of the fiscal year, up from 3.36% at the end of the prior fiscal year, according to the Treasury Department. Meanwhile, the deficit as a share the nation’s economy was more than 6% in the last fiscal year, according to Treasury’s rough estimate. That’s more than twice Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s goal. Big, beautiful bill impact The Republicans’ sweeping tax cuts are also starting to have an effect. Although many businesses are raking in higher profits, gross corporate tax revenue declined by $43 billion, or 9%. The “big, beautiful bill” allowed companies to take larger deductions for certain investments. Most of the “big, beautiful bill’s” historic cuts – notably to Medicaid – don’t start kicking in until next year. At the same time, Social Security benefits are becoming more costly as the nation ages, which also contributed to the widening gap between revenue and spending. Lawmakers will likely have another chance to address the nation’s fiscal problems next year, when the US is once again expected to hit the debt ceiling. CNN’s John Towfighi contributed to this report.

articles.title: Reliance Industries to Elon Musk: Competition welcome, but follow rules
articles.summary: New Delhi: Ahead of its Rs 30,213-crore Jio IPO, Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries has rebutted Elon Musk’s tirade on X and said it welcomed competition.
articles.body: New Delhi: Ahead of its Rs 30,213-crore Jio IPO, Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries has rebutted Elon Musk’s tirade on X and said it welcomed competition.Last Wednesday, Musk had accused “certain oligarchs” of “blocking” Starlink’s entry into India before naming Ambani over the next two days in a series of posts.In an early morning statement on Friday, Reliance Industries said: “We welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink. Every player, Jio included, must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land.”“At Reliance, we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best. Jio itself entered India’s crowded telecom market in 2016 as the newest player, with not a single customer. In just 10 years, Jio has earned the trust of over 53 crore customers and given Indians some of the best digital infrastructure and most affordable data in the world,” the statement said.It added: “Like every Indian enterprise, Reliance has grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international, that improve the lives of the people. That openness rests on the rule of law. As govt of India has stated, it applies the same process to every applicant, Indian or foreign. Jio’s own satellite services await clearances.”Govt had also denied Musk’s charges. Last Thursday, Union communications minister Jyotiraditya Scindia had said at India Mobile Congress: “There is a lot of conversation about a particular party (Starlink). But there are three parties that have got licences… As and when govt decides the charge system on revenue basis, spectrum will be assigned to them and as and when they individually fulfil security conditions, then they can start operations.”Sunil Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, Ambani’s Reliance Jio and Musk’s Starlink have got licences and are preparing to start satcom service here so that even remote areas where laying ground infra for broadband is not possible can get the same.
